Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa's governor-elect, who won't be sworn into office until January. The Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP). Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation. item.title: Inception - possibly a ShinyHunters reboot - claims seven victims in a week
item.description: Don't mind the recent arrests. The ShinyHunters extortion gang may still be operating, just under the new name of Inception, according to Okta's threat intelligence group. ShinyHunters is the brash cybercriminal group that, most recently, breached rival gang Clop before hacking the FBI , resulting in at least three arrests of key suspects in September and October. The crims - and their old data leak site - have since gone dark. “While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion,” Okta threat hunters Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels said on Monday. Okta tracks this threat cluster as O-UNC-053 - the “O-UNC” prefix stands for an Okta Uncategorized cluster, and it uses this label before formally attributing the activity to a named threat group. While Okta hasn't formally confirmed O-UNC-053 to be the same crime crew as ShinyHunters, the identity and access management provider’s researchers note that it does use nearly identical social engineering tactics: voice phishing , during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA). Plus, they note: O-UNC-053 operators change the themes of their phishing domains about every four to six weeks, and they also post claimed victims on ShinyHunters’ data leak site. In November, however, organizations targeted by O-UNC-053 began appearing on a new data leak site branded as Inception and not ShinyHunters. The first five - Advanced Micro Devices, Cigna Healthcare, Paychex, PepsiCo, and Henry Schein - appeared November 17 on the site, and all were marked “leaked.” Soon after, security maven Dominic Alvieri questioned if Inception was linked to ShinyHunters. “ShinyHunters are not all in jail,” he wrote on social media. On November 19, AutoZone appeared on the site, with Inception again claiming to have leaked the auto-parts retailer's files. On Saturday, EV technology firm Lucid Group joined the claimed victims. None of the seven companies have confirmed breaches, and none responded to The Register ’s inquiries. We will update this story when we receive more information. Okta Threat Intelligence “is unable to validate if published data is authentic,” the researchers said in response to our questions. In the Monday report, the Okta team does note that Inception’s new data leak site listings “included multiple targets for which Okta Threat Intelligence previously observed O-UNC-053 infrastructure registration.” The infrastructure was registered between six and 19 days before Inception listed the companies on its leak site, and this gap “is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors,” Diallo and Nickels added. The new chip also makes Siri more responsive, so you can get answers to questions with less waiting around. It’s not all about AI, though. The Series 12 also features redesigned health sensors that can now track your heart rate every five seconds even when you’re not exercising, which is particularly help if you have a chronic condition and need to keep a closer eye on your heart rate. It also introduces a new readiness score to help you decide how prepared your body is for the day. Other highlights include easier navigation with simple pinch gestures, and faster charging, which helps to make up for the fact that battery life is rated at up to 24 hours on a single charge, just like the previous-generation model. In our testing, the watch went from 20 to 64 percent charge in just 20 minutes, making it relatively easy to top up while showering or getting ready for the day. item.description:
Tariq is the Editor-in-Chief of Space.com based out of our New York City office and joined the team in 2001, first as an intern and staff writer, and later as an editor. He covers human spaceflight, exploration and space science, as well as skywatching and entertainment. He became Space.com's Managing Editor in 2009 and Editor-in-Chief in 2019. In October 2022, Tariq received the Harry Kolcum Award for excellence in space reporting from the National Space Club Florida Committee. In June 2025, the National Space Society awarded him the Space Pioneer Award for Excellence in Mass Media at the International Space Development Conference in Orlando, Florida.

Hailing from Stockton, California (where he attended the same high school as NASA astronaut Jose Hernandez), Tariq studied print journalism and astronomy at the University of Southern California in Los Angeles, earning a bachelor's degree in journalism in 1999 along with a minor in astronomy. He then served as a staff reporter for The Los Angeles Times covering education and city beats in La Habra and Fullerton in Orange County for the Our Times sections.

In 2000, Tariq became the city reporter for the Huntington Beach Independent, a weekly publication of the Los Angeles Times, covering local politics and events, crime, business and environmental issues. He left the Los Angeles Times in 2001 to study science journalism at New York University, where he earned a master's degree in 2002 from NYU's Science and Environmental Reporting Program (now the Science, Health and Environmental Reporting Program) under the direction of space reporter William Burrows.

Tariq first joined Space.com as an intern in September 2001 while also serving as a research assistant for nutrition writer Gary Taubes and writing freelance projects, where his work appeared in The Scientist and Laboratory Equipment Magazine. He became a full-time reporter covering spaceflight in 2004, with this first launch being NASA's STS-114 Return to Flight mission in July 2005.

Tariq is also an Eagle Scout (yes, he has the Space Exploration merit badge) and went to Space Camp four times as a kid and a fifth time as an adult. When not writing about space, you can find Tariq watching the latest Star Trek TV series, sci-fi movies and reading about hippos, his favorite animal. You can find Tariq at Space.com and as the co-host to the This Week In Space podcast with space historian Rod Pyle on the TWiT network. To see his latest project, you can follow Tariq on Twitter @tariqjmalik.

item.title: Amazon scoops up AI accelerator tech to keep chips busy at all times
item.description: Amazon has agreed to buy AI optimization technology from an Israeli startup in a bid to speed up its inference operations. The house of Bezos on Monday announced a deal to purchase proprietary AI acceleration tech from Decart AI, known as the Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), for an undisclosed amount. Amazon also plans to bring Decart’s three founders and their engineering team into the fold. Decart’s DOS is designed to push AI hardware closer to its maximum performance across different AI models and hardware platforms. The company claims that most AI chips live their lives without reaching their full potential – practically a sin in this age of increased hardware costs and limited availability – and DOS aims to fix that by operating between the model and the chip, optimizing kernels, compilers, and runtimes for the underlying hardware “so every core stays busy.” DOS is hardware-agnostic, with Decart saying it supports Nvidia GPUs, Google TPUs, and, most critically for our purposes here, AWS Trainium chips. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost,” Peter DeSantis, Amazon SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, and quantum computing, said in the announcement. “That's the pillar Trainium and our AI efforts are built on, and from our earliest work with Decart, we knew they … would help us push it even further.” Decart doesn’t offer much in the way of details about its proprietary AI-maxxing tech, but claims it can reduce latency, improve throughput, and reduce the costs associated with training and inference runs. An Amazon spokesperson clarified to The Register that the deal is an asset purchase and not a full company acquisition, with Amazon only acquiring DOS and the tech behind it as well as personnel. As for what may become of Decart after the deal, that’s unclear. Amazon told us to reach out to Decart to learn what may happen to any remaining employees and the company’s other technology, but we didn’t hear back. Along with offering its optimization stack, Decart has a couple of different AI models: Lucy, a live video model marketed toward advertisers, live streamers, and the like; and Oasis, a world model AI marketed toward companies working on embodied AI applications. Decart’s non-DOS assets weren’t mentioned in the press release, and per the Amazon spokesperson we talked to, that means they weren’t part of the deal. We can’t imagine that the Decart team is too upset about the potential abandonment of those models, though: While neither company has disclosed a price, Bloomberg claims its sources value the deal at around $7.5 billion. If Bloomberg's figure is accurate, that would make this deal one of the most expensive in Amazon’s history, right between its $3.9 billion acquisition of One Medical and its $8.5 billion purchase of film studio MGM . ®

item.title: NASA Awards Contract for NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network Program
item.description: Credit: NASA NASA, on behalf of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), has awarded a contract to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation for the Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) instruments on NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) satellites. The cost-plus-fixed-fee, firm-fixed-price, and time-and-materials hybrid contract has a value of $290.6 million. The period of performance runs from Nov. 23 through April 1, 2042. The work will take place at the awardee’s facility. Under the contract, Northrop Grumman will provide the design, development, production, testing, and mission support for three SMBA instruments, the next generation of low Earth orbit microwave sounders. NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, is managing the acquisition, and NOAA will own and operate the instruments and deliver the data to users worldwide. Microwave sounders provide critical measurements of temperature and moisture in the atmosphere, which significantly influence weather patterns. The SMBA instruments could improve the medium-range forecasts for NOAA’s National Weather Service. The NEON mission is a collaboration between NASA and NOAA. The mission is led by NOAA, which provides funding, technical requirements, and postlaunch operations. NASA will manage the development of the NEON satellites and launch them for NOAA. NASA and NOAA will work with commercial partners to design and build the NEON spacecraft and instruments. item.title: Strive (ASST) Buys No Bitcoin Last Week, Holdings Stay at 43,404 BTC
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Strive (ASST) Buys No Bitcoin Last Week, Holdings Stay at 43,404 BTC Strive (Nasdaq: ASST) bought no bitcoin last week and sold no stock to fund new purchases, leaving its holdings unchanged at 43,404 BTC, according to a Monday 8-K filing. The Dallas-based company reported that its bitcoin count was unchanged between Nov. 13 and Nov. 20. It sold no Class A common shares, no SATA preferred shares and no SATS preferred shares in its at-the-market programs from the Nov. 13 close through the Nov. 20 close. Strive pauses after two small buys The pause follows a slowdown from the October sprint that built the stack. Strive bought 251 bitcoin for $17.5 million the prior week at an average of $69,853 per coin, after adding just 29 coins the week before that. Bitcoin traded near $61,000 on Coinbase on Monday afternoon. That is about 12.6% below the $69,853 average Strive paid for its most recent purchase. At that price, the 43,404-coin stack is worth roughly $2.65 billion. The filing gives no reason for the pause, and the company has not said whether it plans to resume weekly buying. Strive has typically disclosed its holdings on Mondays, so next week’s update will show whether the stack grows again. Most of the stack was built quickly. Strive held 28,000 bitcoin on Sept. 30 and acquired 15,124 more between Oct. 1 and Oct. 30, including a single 6,182-coin purchase. The company closed a registered offering of 7 million SATS shares on Oct. 20 for about $609 million in net proceeds, which funded much of that run. Cash and preferred holdings Strive’s cash and cash equivalents slipped to $462.4 million as of Nov. 20 from $465.3 million a week earlier, a decline of $2.9 million. The filing does not break out what drove the change. The company also still holds 505,000 shares of Strategy’s variable-rate STRC preferred stock. The fair value of that position fell to $47.3 million from $50.5 million, a drop of about $3.2 million, with the share count unchanged. Share counts were also flat. Strive reported 118,133,002 Class A shares and 9,198,107 Class B shares, for 127,331,109 effective common shares. Outstanding preferred stood at 14,030,176 shares of SATA and 7,141,037 shares of SATS, the 15% perpetual preferred it has used to fund most of its purchases. Strive’s holdings rose from 43,153 bitcoin on Nov. 6 to 43,404 on Nov. 13, and the filing shows no change since. With no common or preferred stock sold, the company raised no new capital through its offering programs last week, which left cash as its main resource for dividends and operations. Shares rally, then fade with the market Strive shares were trading near $15.55 at 3:56 p.m. ET on Monday, up about 7.1% from Friday’s close of $14.51, according to Yahoo Finance. The stock opened near $17.64, a gain of more than 20%, and gave back much of it through the session. item.title: Bitcoin Price Fades Near $61,000 as Stocks Soar on Huang’s Return
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Bitcoin Price Fades Near $61,000 as Stocks Soar on Huang’s Return The bitcoin price slipped back to near $61,100 on Monday afternoon, giving up nearly all of its morning spike even as Wall Street held one of its biggest rallies in years on Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. Bitcoin jumped above $64,000 shortly after the Nvidia news broke before 10 a.m. ET and topped out near $64,500. The move reversed within hours , and the bitcoin price dipped to around $60,800 by 2:45 p.m. ET. It remains up only modestly on the day. The round trip was costly for leveraged traders. Bitcoin liquidations reached about $321 million , with short bets making up $224 million of that total. Liquidations across the broader crypto market topped $762 million. Stocks hold gains as bitcoin fades Stocks kept climbing while bitcoin slid. The Nasdaq Composite was up about 6.9% near 24,170 at about 3:40 p.m. ET, while the S&P 500 gained about 5% and the Dow rose about 3.2%. The S&P 500 had fallen seven straight days before Monday. Nvidia (NVDA) led the move, trading near $165.66, up about 32% from Friday’s close of $125.53. The board voted unanimously to bring Huang back as president, CEO and director, 12 days after he resigned. A stronger dollar may be weighing on the bitcoin price. The dollar index rose about 0.65% to 104.40 , its strongest level since April 2025, as the stock rebound put more Federal Reserve rate hikes back in play. The Fed meets Dec. 8-9, and a quarter-point hike remains the base case. Adam Haeems, head of asset management at Tesseract Group, pointed to steady selling during U.S. market hours since Huang first stepped down. “Bitcoin has fallen in seven of the eight U.S. sessions since Huang went, today’s included, and last week each session’s fall lined up with that day’s ETF outflow,” he said. Crypto stocks keep most of their gains Crypto stocks held up far better than the bitcoin price. Strategy (MSTR) was up about 9.3% near $85.03 in afternoon trading, after it disclosed a purchase of 457 bitcoin last week. Coinbase (COIN) gained about 6.7% to near $108.78, Robinhood (HOOD) rose about 8.8% to near $67.64 and Circle (CRCL) added about 8% to near $51.33. Miners with AI data center businesses posted the biggest moves. IREN (IREN) jumped about 23% to near $14.57, CleanSpark (CLSK) rose about 12.6% and MARA Holdings (MARA) gained about 10%. Core Scientific (CORZ) climbed about 9.4% and Riot Platforms (RIOT) added about 7.1%. ETF flows and inflation data are next Monday’s spot bitcoin ETF flows are the next test. The funds lost about $1.79 billion last week, their fourth straight week of net outflows, as bitcoin slid toward $58,000 on Friday and hit a weekend low near $55,100. “Tonight’s ETF flow figure is the first real test of this bounce,” Haeems said. item.title: Surveillance pricing uses our personal data to make us pay more
item.description: “It costs what it costs” is a mindset I’ve found useful when encountering a sizable, but highly necessary or desired, expense. The sentiment encourages me to accept the price because that’s the accepted value of the gadget, app, or service that I really need or want. But with surveillance pricing, that comfort is no longer a given. I could end up paying more for my TV because of where I am or more for a software subscription because of my age. Surveillance pricing leverages data collected from our web history , smart devices , and apps with the goal of getting us to pay more. That obfuscates the value of products, challenges smart shopping and budgets, and makes it harder for people to get products and services at a fair price. Read full article Comments

item.title: Bluetooth brakes are broken as researchers find anyone can control them
item.description: Imagine something as mission-critical as the brakes on a trailer being vulnerable to unauthorized control. One Australian manufacturer made the interesting choice of building Bluetooth into a trailer brake controller without adequately securing its critical braking functions. Anyone within Bluetooth range of an unpatched Elecbrakes trailer controller could potentially trigger its brakes or apply more braking force than intended, without needing to authenticate. The discovery comes courtesy of a pair of security researchers from Element Digital, Patrick Forck and Jeremy McCarthy. Their investigation began earlier this year when Forck was driving down the road and noticed that his physical Elecbrakes In-Car Remote had connected to someone else's trailer without pairing or prompting him. “It had connected mid-drive, without pairing or a prompt, to a brake controller that wasn’t mine, on a trailer I’d never seen, belonging to a driver who had no idea,” the researchers wrote . That one-off connection triggered a full-scale investigation by the pair. For those unfamiliar with trailer brake controllers, these devices are commonly used on larger trailers. Australian manufacturer Elecbrakes sells such controllers in Australia and New Zealand. Depending on jurisdiction, trailers over a certain weight are required to have their own braking system, which Elecbrakes manufactures. Elecbrakes offers two versions that are designed to be easier to install than traditional controllers: One that’s mounted in a vehicle, and one that is mounted directly on a trailer. That trailer-mounted unit can receive Bluetooth commands from the Elecbrakes smartphone app or a separate in-car remote. Given the importance of such control units to road safety, it’s easy to imagine how serious such a vulnerability could be if it proved to be easy to exploit, and boy, did it. Forck and McCarthy admitted they’re infrastructure security guys, not software devs, so they turned to Claude Code to dissect a decompiled copy of the Elecbrakes app, which Claude was happy to oblige. “What came back from the analysis was a map of the device’s entire Bluetooth GATT profile: 47 characteristics across four services, commands sent as plain unencrypted byte arrays, no checksums, no sequence numbers,” the researchers noted. To make matters worse, there was no authentication required for critical braking commands, even though other Bluetooth functions required pairing. Claude then built a web app that ran in Chrome which was able to access the Bluetooth controls for a nearby Elecbrakes system, and they were able to modify practically every aspect of brake control on a unit owned by one of them. Pairing failed on a few attempts, but not where it mattered: It allowed the connection without issue for actual brake control. They sent a few bytes to the brake control characteristic, and were shocked. “The electromagnetic hum at the brake drums was immediate and, frankly, a little sickening,” the pair said. “I

item.title: Reports: Russia may launch nuclear weapon into orbit as soon as next month
item.description: Western intelligence officials worry that Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite into orbit before the end of the year, suggesting the country's development of a satellite-killing weapon of mass destruction is more advanced than previously thought, German media reported Monday. The orbiting nuclear weapon would threaten thousands of satellites in low-Earth orbit, including military and commercial communications networks like Starshield and Starlink. A nuclear-armed satellite would also put at risk Western military surveillance satellites and human spaceflight platforms like the International Space Station. A nuclear detonation in orbit would be indiscriminate, also knocking out Russia's own spacecraft and Chinese satellites. US lawmakers briefed on government intelligence first disclosed Russia's ambition to deploy a space-based nuclear weapon in early 2024 . At the time, US officials said Russia had launched a test satellite in 2022 to test the effects of radiation on space hardware and pave the way for a future nuclear-armed craft, but that Russia had not yet sent a nuclear weapon into orbit. item.title: How sci‑fi imagines sports in microgravity, and how zero‑g sports might actually work
item.description:
Alan Bradley is an experienced tech and culture writer with more than 20 years covering gaming, tech, and hardware. He has served as commerce director and in senior editorial roles at major publications. His work has appeared in Rolling Stone, U.S. News & World Report, PCMag, TechRadar, GamesRadar+, CNET, Live Science, Variety, and many other outlets. Alan is also a novelist—his debut novel, the urban fantasy The Sixth Borough, is available now.

Sports in space have a long and proud tradition, whether it's Alan Shepard playing golf on the moon or the crew of the ISS hosting their own version of the Summer Olympics . The future looks bright as well, with the foundation of the Space Games Federation , the self-described "first governing and sanctioning body for competitive sports played in zero or micro-gravity," co-founded by a NASA astronaut. Not to be outdone, science fiction has expanded the idea of zero-g and low-gravity sports to their logical extent, imagining everything from Doctor Who's zero-g squash to the advanced, gamified combat simulations of Ender's Game. There was even Space Jam 's alien basketball game for the fate of the planet, though the gravity-defying antics there come from cartoon shenanigans rather than a zero-g playing field. As humanity edges closer to colonizing our neighbors through projects like the Artemis Program and its ambition to establish habitats on the moon, our imaginations have to expand to encompass not only how we'll live in space but also how we'll play. The rules change when gravity disappears (Image credit: Zero-G) We rarely think about it in an Earth context, but every sport is heavily influenced by gravity. It defines how balls arc, how quickly players can move, and even how we orient ourselves in play spaces. Remove the gravity, and all of those assumptions and mechanics evaporate as well. "First of all, in zero g, Isaac Newton will win every time," Les Johnson, former Chief Technologist for NASA, told Space. Les is a physicist with over 35 years of experience working at Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, as well as a science fiction author. "'For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction,'" quotes Johnson. "This is very difficult to simulate in real life due to gravity; special effects often try to compensate. With today’s AI and green screens, it can actually look good on screen." In a microgravity scenario, the concept of up and down is no longer relevant. Suddenly, the playing field expands from a single, fixed plane to a fully three-dimensional space that includes height. (Image credit: Netflix) Momentum is also a completely different beast. Instead of being able to quickly stop and pivot the way you can during terrestrial sports, once you start moving in microgravity, you keep going until something stops you. It takes the trickiness of moving on ice in sports like hockey and increases it by several orders of magnitude. Of course, the havoc wouldn't stop with m

item.title: Bitdeer Sells All 281 Bitcoin It Mined Last Week, Holds None
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Bitdeer Sells All 281 Bitcoin It Mined Last Week, Holds None Bitdeer sold every bitcoin it mined last week and still holds none of its own, the company said in its latest weekly update, continuing a nearly year-long strategy of turning production into cash after a weekend plunge in the bitcoin price. The Singapore-based miner reported output of 281.1 BTC and sales of 281.1 BTC for the week, for a net addition of zero. Its pure holdings, which exclude customer deposits, were zero as of Nov. 20. The sales came as bitcoin fell to a weekend low of $55,106 early Saturday at 1:17 AM ET, Bitcoin Magazine Pro data shows. The price has since bounced to near $62,700 as of 11:23 AM ET Monday. Bitdeer’s reserve has been drained all year Bitdeer’s treasury shrank from roughly 2,000 BTC at the end of 2025 to zero by Feb. 20, when Bitcoin Magazine reported the miner had liquidated its reserve over eight weeks. At the time, the company said the move should not be a concern for the broader market. Bitdeer’s filings show how little it has kept since. In its third-quarter results, filed with the SEC on a Form 6-K on Nov. 10, the company listed 47 BTC held at Sept. 30, down from 2,029 a year earlier. Its September production update showed 61 BTC held at the end of August. The company mined 1,355 BTC in September and 3,855 BTC in the third quarter, compared with 1,109 BTC in the same quarter of 2025. Self-mining margins stay thin Bitdeer has grown its fleet quickly. Self-mining hashrate reached 82.3 exahashes per second in the third quarter, up from 35.0 a year earlier, with another 28.7 exahashes per second of co-mining at third-party sites, the quarterly report shows . The economics are tight. Self-mining generated $217.5 million in revenue in the quarter but only $6.2 million in gross profit. Electricity averaged $47 per megawatt-hour, and the fleet ran at 15.4 joules per terahash. Bitdeer posted record revenue of $320.7 million and adjusted EBITDA of $69.6 million, but a net loss of $125.5 million. That included a $54.6 million non-cash loss tied to a bitcoin-collateralized loan from a related party. Bitdeer also reported $213.7 million in cash and restricted cash, and its board authorized a new $100 million share repurchase program on Oct. 8. Borrowing against coins instead of selling them Not every miner is selling. American Bitcoin secured a $150 million revolving credit line from FalconX on Monday that is backed by its bitcoin. The company said the facility lets it raise cash without drawing down its reserve. The loan carries a 5.95% fee and an initial collateral ratio of 143%. Fully drawing it would require about $214.5 million in pledged bitcoin. American Bitcoin has not said whether it has drawn on the line, and its release lists the risk that pledged coins could be liquidated if prices fall. item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 23, 2015: Blue Origin sticks 1st-ever rocket landing from space with its suborbital New Shepard rocket
item.description: null On Nov. 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing. Before this time, all rockets were single-use only — even SpaceX's rockets. Blue Origin changed the concept forever. After launching the New Shepard capsule safely into space, the rocket started heading back to Earth. It flew towards a landing pad, reignited its engine to slow down and touched down softly on the ground . This was the first successful vertical landing from space in history. The Blue Origin milestone meant that rockets could be reused for multiple missions, which saves money and reduces waste. (Image credit: Blue Origin) Why it mattered Today, SpaceX may be the most well-known for landing its Falcon 9 rocket boosters from orbit. The company's triple-core Falcon Heavy boosters can also land vertically and its massive Starship megarocket can even return to the launch site to be caught by giant metal arms. But in the end, Blue Origin did it first. Blue Origin's New Shepard booster landing kicked off an era of vertical launch and vertical landings for rockets that continues to this day. It may have even outlasted the New Shepard rocket. Since that first landing, Blue Origin has launched 17 suborbital astronaut flights with New Shepard, and 21 more uncrewed flights for a total of 38 missions between April 2015 and 2026. The company reused its New Shepard boosters repeatedly (though it did lose one during an uncrewed launch after a technical issue.) But in January 2026, the company announced a pause in New Shepard flights for two years so that it could focus on moon lander projects. But Blue Origin did not abandon rocket landings. Indeed, the company's success with New Shepard led it to build vertical landing into its larger orbital rocket, New Glenn, which made its first successful landing 2025 — nearly 10 years after that first touchdown. Blue Origin has since reflown a New Glenn booster , and is developing a new rocket engine called Northstar for even better performance. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: Critical Cisco remote code execution bug under attack
item.description: Attackers are currently exploiting a critical vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-76466 in Cisco Expressway that allows them to remotely execute commands as root without any authentication, according to warnings from the US government and security researchers. CVE-2026-76466 , which carries a 9.8 CVSS rating, affects Cisco Expressway-C and Cisco Expressway-E gateways configured in clusters, both virtual and physical appliances running vulnerable software. These provide firewall traversal, VPN-less remote access, and call routing for remote users connecting to voice, video, and messaging collaboration services. The bug involves hard-coded authentication credentials and insufficient certificate validation in clustered Expressway deployments. “An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands,” Cisco said in October, when it disclosed the bug and issued a software update that fixed the flaw. “A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device.” At the time, the networking vendor said it wasn’t aware of any abuse of the vulnerability. That all changed late last week, however, when Russian security firm F6 said it was investigating “the first observed case” of miscreants exploiting CVE-2026-76466, shortly after a public proof-of-concept exploit became available. “The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices,” F6’s Cyber Defense Center said on Thursday. “Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization’s internal network. After obtaining root access, the attackers began preparing tooling for further lateral movement across the infrastructure.” Specifically, the criminals prepared custom Python code to scan the victim’s network and identify files and folders shared over the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. The scripts were also designed to interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories for credentials and other sensitive information. The Python scripts used in the attack indicated that the operator used an AI assistant, according to F6. The security shop also noted that one of the key indicators of compromise is a nodeup “wombat@127.0.0.1” entry in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices. A day later, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-76466 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and told federal agencies to patch by Monday. Cisco updated its advisory on Monday to acknowledge CISA’s addition, while noting that it has no direct evidence of active exploitation. The Register reached out to the networking and security vendor for additional details about the scope of the attacks, but did not receive any response. We will update this story as we learn more. ®

item.title: Solo Bitcoin Miner Wins $191,000 Block Reward With Just 11 TH/s
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Solo Bitcoin Miner Wins $191,000 Block Reward With Just 11 TH/s A solo miner running about 11 terahashes per second has mined Bitcoin block 977,057, collecting a reward of 3.1287 BTC, or about $191,000, on a machine that makes up roughly one-millionth of a percent of the network. The block was found through the solo service at CKpool on Sunday, Nov. 22, at about 7:54 a.m. ET. The reward is the 3.125 BTC subsidy plus about 0.0037 BTC in transaction fees, and it was worth roughly $191,000 at bitcoin’s price when the block landed. How the solo block played out The block holds 584 transactions. Its coinbase transaction pays 3.0661 BTC to a single address and 0.0626 BTC, about 2% of the reward, to a second output. That split matches the service’s 2% fee, which means the miner’s take is a little over $186,000. Con Kolivas, the developer behind CKpool, congratulated the miner on X, whose address he abbreviated as bc1q~zy9j. It matches the end of the address that received the payout. Kolivas called it the 323rd block found on the service and “yet another lucky one.” He said the miner had only about 11.1 TH/s of hashrate on a 3.47 TH worker. “A miner of this size has about a one in 1650 chance of solving a block in a year,” Kolivas wrote. The block was tagged to Solo CK on the mempool.space block explorer, and its coinbase carries the pool’s signature. CKpool describes itself as a service that lets miners go after full solo blocks without running their own node, since you cannot mine directly to a Bitcoin Core node. A recent run of solo wins Solo CK has found five blocks since Nov. 6, according to the explorer’s pool page . The most recent before this one was block 976,642 on Nov. 19, followed by blocks on Nov. 11, Nov. 7 and Nov. 6. Each paid between 3.13 and 3.15 BTC. Earlier this year, a different solo miner won block 943,411 on the same service on April 2, for about 3.139 BTC. In October, a FutureBit Apollo solo miner found block 973,262 and earned 3.154 BTC. Those wins are the exception. Most of the network’s hashrate sits in large pools and industrial operations that split rewards across many miners, which is how they smooth out the luck. A single small machine can run for years without finding anything, and a lucky block can show up on day one. Miners on the service get nothing unless they find a block, and then they keep the full reward minus the 2% fee. Network hashrate and difficulty Bitcoin’s network hashrate was about 1.04 zettahashes per second, or roughly 1,043 exahashes, on a three-day average Monday. At 11.1 TH/s, the winning miner contributes about 0.000001% of that total, which fits Kolivas’s odds. One in 1,650 works out to a chance of about 0.06% over a full year of mining. Mining difficulty is about 134.8 trillion. The last adjustment cut it by about 9.1%, and the next one, expected around Nov. 26, is estimated to raise it by about 9.2%, according to mempool.space. item.title: Bulgaria evicts cyber snoops who lurked inside government networks for 5 years
item.description: The Ancient Thracian heartland of Bulgaria says it has shut down a cyberespionage operation that gave intruders access to government networks for five years – the longest-running known campaign against its administration. Bulgaria's Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation said the unauthorized and officially unattributed attackers first gained access to infrastructure used by government institutions to exchange information in 2021. It explained that the intrusion went unnoticed for so long because "the previous means of protection did not work as a single, integrated system," and that without a new, recently installed product, it may have gone undetected for much longer. "The incident was discovered thanks to the new national cybersecurity system, which for the first time provides a single picture of what is happening in state networks," the ministry added. "Without it, this activity would most likely have remained hidden for an indefinite period of time." Bulgaria acknowledged that "sensitive information related to the work of the state" was accessed, but did not specify the scale of the compromise. Innovation and Digital Transformation Minister Ivan Vasilev said attackers had downloaded more than 130 GB of data over five years. He also put the volume at 62 million pages. The Register contacted the Bulgarian government for confirmation of these numbers. The ministry said that it has not yet found any evidence that citizens' personal data was compromised, and that the affected infrastructure "will be under increased surveillance for 90 days" in case the attackers try to regain access. Vasilev said multiple international hacking groups had accessed government systems since 2021. He did not specify the names of these groups, however, nor did he name any specific countries that may have been involved. In a follow-up interview with bTV , Vasilev blamed political instability and frequent changes of ministerial leadership for leaving government systems inadequately protected. A representative of the Progressive Bulgaria party, which back in May won Bulgaria's eighth general election in five years, Vasilev said the "constant change of leadership" means "important things for the state do not actually happen." Vasilev said the intrusion was discovered over the summer as the national cybersecurity system was upgraded, and that teams had spent the past three to four months removing the attackers. ®

item.title: Weird 'potato chips' and 'ghostly rocks' on Mars spotted by NASA rovers Curiosity and Perseverance
item.description: null NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have spotted a bizarre assortment of Martian oddities, from potato chip-like rocks and ghostly white formations to mysterious patterns etched into the Red Planet's surface. While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years. In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life. NASA's Curiosity rover recently wrapped up a drilling campaign at a location nicknamed "Nazca," where scientists have been examining unusual disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in the surrounding bedrock. Some of the features are so thin and flat that the mission team likened them to potato chips, according to a statement from the space agency. NASA's Curiosity rover captured a close-up view of unusual, disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in Martian bedrock using its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI) on Nov. 7, 2026 (Sol 5067). The thin, flattened formations resemble tiny potato chips. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS) Curiosity used its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), mounted on the end of its robotic arm, to capture detailed close-up images of the formations on Nov. 7 — the rover's 5,067th Martian day , or Sol 5067. The rover also used its ChemCam instrument to study the rocks' chemical composition, while samples from the Nazca drill site were delivered to its onboard Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument for further analysis. Meanwhile, NASA's Perseverance rover has been investigating a collection of unusually bright rocks in an area called "Idubi," located in the “Lac de Charmes” region outside Jezero Crater. The rover captured images of the formations on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023), revealing pale, ghostly-looking rocks that stand out dramatically against the darker, dust-covered Martian landscape. Data from Perseverance's SuperCam instrument revealed that the rocks are rich in hydrated silica rather than being typical igneous rocks. That discovery has scientists particularly interested. On Earth, hydrated silica can form in environments involving hydrothermal activity or groundwater. These deposits are also capable of preserving microscopic fossils, making them valuable targets in the search for evidence of ancient life, according to another statement from NASA. NASA's Perseverance rover captured unusually bright, silica-rich rock in the "Idubi" area outside Jezero Crater on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023), using its left Mastcam-Z camera. The pale formation stands out against the darker, dust-covered Martian terrain. item.title: Microsoft mega outage: Report reveals testing gaps and emails that never arrived
item.description: Some emails never reached their recipients during November's Microsoft 365 outage, the company has confirmed in a final report that also exposes gaps in its testing and recovery procedures. The post-incident report details how a Windows defect brought down Exchange Online and disrupted features across other Microsoft 365 services. For affected users, the cloud became someone else's unavailable computer. A preliminary report had already blamed a July code change, combined with a failover and reduced capacity. The final report confirms those findings and sets out Microsoft's plans to improve change auditing and recovery procedures, and add spare capacity. The defect affected Microsoft's gateway server configuration, not standard Windows deployments. The epic outage (named the "Microsoft long weekend" by some wags) kicked off on November 12 and wasn't fully resolved until November 14. Microsoft extended its delivery retry window to 48 hours, but some delayed messages destined for consumer mailboxes inactive for more than 30 days still expired, generating non-delivery reports. The company said all queued enterprise messages were eventually delivered, with none found permanently lost. The report is grim, particularly in how the failure ramped up as US users came online to find gateway servers toppling over. At the worst point, more than 80 percent of North American gateway servers were unresponsive. The problem proved elusive, and it took Microsoft some time to identify the change and deploy a fix. Microsoft has had a week to ponder what it did and did not do, and the report has some next steps to avoid a repeat of November's events. Some are obvious, and some are a little surprising. Working to reduce the blast radius of failures is an obvious one, and actions include partitioning and isolation to ensure failures can be contained before taking down traffic globally. Recovery procedures also need improvement, along with communication and capacity to ensure there is sufficient headroom. Microsoft's load tests used older, lower-core-count hardware, making them less likely to expose a defect that worsened on newer machines. The company now plans to test newer hardware with more realistic traffic and peak loads, and broaden its failover testing. Microsoft also plans to improve diagnostics and change auditing so engineers can identify troublesome Windows changes faster. July's defect had been running worldwide for more than three months before it brought the gateways down. ®

item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Nvidia Soars as Huang Returns, Lifting Stocks and Crypto Shares Nvidia shares jumped about 35% on Monday after the chipmaker reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO, restoring roughly $1 trillion in market value at the open. The stock traded near $169.20 at 10:41 a.m. ET, up from Friday’s close of $125.53, and Wall Street rallied with it. The board voted unanimously to bring Huang back, effective immediately, after what it called a series of discussions and meetings. It said it received input from “senior levels of the United States government” and is confident his return “poses no national security risk.” President Donald Trump had urged the move. Several items remain open. An independent board committee will finish its investigation into reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, and Huang said he will cooperate. Nvidia also formed a national security and export control committee and is searching for a chief compliance officer. From resignation to reversal Huang resigned on Nov. 11, days after admitting an affair with a woman U.S. officials believe is linked to Chinese intelligence. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress became interim CEO and Harvey Jones became board chair. Nvidia had said it was searching for a permanent successor. The stock slid for seven straight weeks, the longest such streak since 2008. On Friday it plunged 14% after Reuters reported that the SEC is examining the company’s accounting practices. Reuters noted that investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing. Huang’s return reverses most of the losses since his affair became public. The selloff came even after Nvidia reported better-than-expected quarterly results on Nov. 17. For weeks, the board had said it was not considering bringing Huang back, which makes Monday’s announcement a sharp turn for the world’s most closely watched chipmaker. Wall Street and chip stocks rally The Nasdaq Composite rose about 7.4% to near 24,300 at 10:41 a.m. ET, and the S&P 500 gained about 5.4% to near 7,280. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed about 3.3%, or more than 1,500 points, to near 49,700. The S&P 500 had fallen seven straight days. Chip stocks followed Nvidia higher. Micron (MU) rose about 21% and Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM) gained about 16%, while Intel (INTC) added about 15%. AMD rose about 9% and Broadcom (AVGO) was up about 3%. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned on Sunday that the Fed may be making a “policy mistake” if it overtightens. The central bank meets Dec. 8-9, and a quarter-point increase remains the base case. Bitcoin and crypto stocks follow The bitcoin price climbed to a Monday high near $64,500, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro data, and was near $63,000 at 10:41 a.m. ET. That is about $8,000 above the weekend low of $55,106, hit at roughly 1:17 a.m. ET on Saturday. Bitcoin had slid with stocks on Friday. Crypto-linked stocks jumped. item.title: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO, board chair
item.description: Nvidia's board of directors has voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman of the board, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of multiple scandals . The reinstatement, announced Monday morning , is "effective immediately" and was based in part on "input from senior levels of the United States government" that assured the board members that "Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk." That assurance comes despite Huang's admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China. It also comes despite multiple developing investigations from multiple different government departments into those and other alleged national security, accounting, and corporate governance failures. item.title: Cross River Bank Launches Its First Bitcoin-Backed Loans With LendingUSA
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Cross River Bank Launches Its First Bitcoin-Backed Loans With LendingUSA Cross River Bank has launched its first bitcoin-backed loans, working with consumer lender LendingUSA to let eligible borrowers take out between $10,000 and $250,000 against their BTC without selling it. The program is the first time Cross River has originated bitcoin-secured loans itself, according to The Block. LendingUSA runs the application platform, and every loan is made by Cross River, a New Jersey state-chartered bank, according to LendingUSA . How the loans work Borrowers can choose a loan-to-value ratio of 30%, 50% or 70%, which sets how much cash they receive against the value of the bitcoin they pledge. LendingUSA defines the ratio as the loan balance divided by the value of the collateral, so a 50% loan against $100,000 of bitcoin would be $50,000. Two repayment options are offered: interest-only or no monthly payments. On an interest-only loan, borrowers make smaller monthly payments that roughly cover interest, with the principal and any remaining interest due at the end of the term. On a no-monthly-payment loan, the full balance plus interest is due at the end. LendingUSA says borrowers can repay early without penalties or fees . Applicants go through a soft credit check, and LendingUSA says approval rests on the crypto being pledged rather than a credit score. The company says funding typically arrives within one to three business days after the collateral is verified. Custody and margin risk A qualified third-party custodian holds the bitcoin for the life of the loan. Once the loan is repaid in full, the collateral is released back to the borrower, according to the company. The terms carry the usual risk of borrowing against a volatile asset. LendingUSA says that if the value of the bitcoin falls, the loan-to-value ratio rises, and borrowers may be asked to add collateral or pay down the debt to avoid liquidation. The company says it will try to notify borrowers first but cannot guarantee it during fast price moves. The timing matters. Bitcoin was trading near $61,000 on Monday morning, so a borrower at the 70% tier would have far less room before a collateral call than one at the 30% tier. Lower ratios leave a bigger cushion but unlock less cash per bitcoin pledged. LendingUSA markets the loans for uses such as debt consolidation, home improvements and large purchases. The company says it has served more than 200,000 borrowers across its lending business, and the crypto product is its first expansion into digital asset-backed loans. A chartered bank joins bitcoin lending Cross River President Evan Russo framed the launch as a natural extension of the bank’s work. “Digital assets have become a meaningful part of how many consumers build and hold wealth, and the financial system must evolve to serve them responsibly,” Russo said in a statement. “Cross River was built on the belief that innovation and trusted infrastructure go hand in hand,”

item.title: 'Avengers: Doomsday' gets final trailer, explaining why Steve Rogers is back and showing an epic battle with the X-Men
item.description: The final trailer for Avengers: Doomsday just landed, and it finally puts the spotlight on our boy Steve Rogers. Avengers: Doomsday has been promising the scale and excitement the MCU has often been lacking since the Infinity Saga. Previous trailers played it safe, mostly setting up the conflict and introducing Victor Von Doom. Now it’s time for one last explosive look at the film before it tries to conquer cinemas next month. Disney and Marvel Studios have just released a "final trailer" that puts the focus back on Steve Rogers — no longer Captain America but still ready to use Mjolnir — and Thor as the veterans leading the New Avengers, former colleagues, the Fantastic Four, and even Fox's X-Men (after some first-encounter fights, of course) against Doom and his followers. A few dodgy CG shots aside, it looks grand, and if you're a big X-Men fan, it's hard not to get goosebumps when Cyclops (James Marsden) finally gets to say the thing. The multiverse-spanning story is still largely kept a secret in this trailer, but at least we get a better sense of what the emotional stakes are for Rogers and how all these heroes can realistically work together against the greatest threat they've faced so far (even if most of them won't get more than a few lines). (Image credit: Marvel) As for Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom, this isn't his trailer, but the mysterious Latverian witches — who have fueled many theories online for months — are finally seen in motion. Doom has, however, received a simple but evocative poster that mirrors one of the original Iron Man ones. Even though Marvel Studios' honcho, Kevin Feige, has shot down the theory that this Victor Von Doom is a Tony Stark variant , you can't stop marketing from doing the obvious things, it seems. We won't complain. (Image credit: Marvel Studios) Avengers: Doomsday won't fix all of the Multiverse Saga's shortcomings, but at the very least, it looks like a proper fun time with more toys being mashed together than ever before and proper stakes. Right before Christmas, it's hard to resist such a pitch. Avengers: Doomsday assembles on December 18, 2026, only in cinemas...Yes, it opens the same day as Dune: Part Three . item.title: British retailer Next downplays data breach at tech supplier
item.description: British retailer Next has become the latest high street name to find itself caught up in a cyberattack, although it insists the data accessed by hackers is "benign" and its customers have nothing to worry about. The clothing and homeware giant told investors on Monday that a third-party supplier had suffered a security breach, allowing an unauthorized party to access information relating to Next. The retailer says its own systems remain untouched and that, so far, there's no evidence that customer personal data has fallen into the wrong hands. "We have been informed that one of our third-party online suppliers has experienced a cyber incident which has resulted in unauthorized access to certain benign data relating to NEXT," the company said in its statement, which it shared with The Register . "We took immediate steps to investigate the nature and scope of the incident with the supplier." The breached supplier provides technology services to Next, and the "benign" information accessed is understood to be low-level data. Sensitive customer details, including addresses, passwords, and banking information, are believed to be unaffected. Next hasn't identified the supplier, explained exactly what the hackers managed to get their hands on, or revealed how much information was accessed, and declined to say when asked by The Register . However, the retailer has seemingly decided that the stolen data won’t be of much use to the criminals responsible. "Our investigations are ongoing; however, current evidence indicates that no customer personal data has been compromised," Next said. "The information affected is limited in nature and, based on our current assessment, cannot be used to facilitate fraud against our customers or NEXT." Next also stressed that its own IT infrastructure had escaped unscathed, saying it was "confident that NEXT’s own systems have not been compromised and that this remains an incident affecting the supplier's environment." Despite repeatedly describing the compromised information as harmless, Next says it is treating the incident "with the utmost seriousness" and is working with the affected supplier, law enforcement, and relevant regulators. The incident comes just weeks after fellow British fashion retailer Asos suffered a breach of its own , with hackers gaining access to customer information through third-party platforms. That attack, which came to light on October 6 when customers received an unauthorized push notification through the Asos app announcing that the company had been hacked, was traced to a social engineering scam. An attacker impersonated a trusted contact to trick an Asos employee into handing over login credentials, which were then used to access external platforms. Asos later admitted that the intruders had accessed customer names, contact details, and some account information, but passwords and payment card details were apparently off limits. Credits: Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Tea Temim (Columbia), Rick Arendt (UMBC), Dan Milisavljevic (Purdue University); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI) NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has painted a vibrant tapestry of the legendary supernova remnant Cassiopeia A (Cas A). Remnants like these are the clouds of gas and dust that remain following the explosion of a massive star and will eventually seed a new generation of stars and planets. This high-resolution, mid-infrared observation from Webb reveals new details that are helping astronomers chronicle the structure and evolution of Cas A’s original star. The Webb data supports a scenario in which the interior of the star underwent a dramatic change, possibly just hours before its demise. These results published Monday in The Astrophysical Journal Letters . Image: Dust In Cassiopeia A (MIRI Image) NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope reveals the hot dust that makes up Cassiopeia A. The composition of its dust provides clues to the structure of Cassiopeia A’s original star. Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Tea Temim (Columbia University), Rick Arendt (UMBC), Dan Milisavljevic (Purdue University); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI) Stars begin their lives as large clouds of mostly hydrogen gas and cosmic dust called molecular clouds. Eventually, gravity causes these molecular clouds to collapse, the material heats up, and protostars — infant stars — form. Under the constant pressure of gravity, hydrogen within a protostar begins to fuse into helium, which marks the point where protostars evolve into full-fledged stars like our Sun. As hydrogen in the core runs out, the core contracts and heats until helium begins to fuse into heavier elements. This process repeats as stars like Cas A’s original star evolve

item.title: The remains of a long-dead volcano on Mars | Space photo of the day for Nov. 23, 2026
item.description: null An image of Tharsis Tholus, a volcano on the surface of Mars, produced by ESA's Mars Express orbiter. (Image credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin) Researchers have spotted an ancient, "dead" Martian volcano from orbit around the Red Planet. What is it? The European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft, which has been orbiting and studying the planet since it arrived in 2003, recently captured incredible new imagery of the volcano Tharsis Tholus. This snapshot was captured by the spacecraft's High Resolution Stereo Camera. Even as old and worn as it is, the Martian volcano stands at around 4.97 miles (8 kilometers) tall which is comparable to some of the highest peaks in the Himalayan mountains. Despite its impressive height, it's still only about a medium-sized volcano for Mars, which is home much more impressively-sized volcanoes. For example, the planet's largest volcano Olympus Mons measures in at roughly 13.2 miles high (21.3 kilometers). Tharsis Tholus, a volcano on the surface of Mars, as seen by ESA's Mars Express orbiter. (Image credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin) Why is it incredible? While Tharsis Tholus might not be the tallest volcano on Mars, it is incredibly steep. It is steeper than Mauna Kea in Hawaii on Earth. To fully showcase the volcano's structure and topography in 3D, researchers actually exaggerated the vertical scale in this image, ESA reported . In addition to being steep and fairly tall, the volcano also has an interesting history. You can see that it is speckled with what look like small holes which are actually craters created by impacts from objects like asteroids. The volcano's current, unique shape is a combined effort by these impacts, environmental factors causing erosion and warping and ancient lava flows that left behind built-up material. The observations by Mars Express also reveals cracks and other imperfections in the volcano. All of these details might seem like superficial bits of detail, however every small crater, every lumpy cliffside and every worn down surface hides information about the planet's past. By studying features like volcanoes on Mars, researchers can piece together what the planet may have looked like in its ancient past. How active was this volcano? How did it interact with the landscape around it? Observations like this can hold the answers.

item.title: Nvidia board puts Jensen Huang back as boss
item.description: There's no telling what caused the Nvidia board to vote unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO less than a week after saying his return wasn’t under consideration – except reportedly the threat of having one's head ripped off and brain peed on – but that really doesn't matter, at least as far as shareholders need to be concerned: Jensen's back in charge and all’s right in the world of chip stocks. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," Huang said of the decision to reinstate him, calling it an honor. Nvidia kicked its former-cum-current CEO and president to the curb on November 12, but not over allegations that he may have been sleeping with a suspected Chinese spy – it was affairs at Nvidia with his subordinates that appears to have been the last straw with Nvidia directors. Nvidia stock has tumbled since Huang’s ouster, and much of the rest of the tech stock world followed suit . Nvidia insiders and tech heavyweights have been pushing for Huang’s return for about as long as he was unemployed, but calls for his return from the US federal government may have been the catalyst for a change of heart among Nvidia leadership who didn’t want Huang back. "In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk," Nvidia said in its statement announcing Huang’s return. "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," board chair Harvey Jones added. Jones was made Nvidia's first board chair upon Huang’s resignation, and will remain in that role. The White House has since confirmed that the senior-level official involved in Huang’s reinstatement was President Trump. According to a White House statement to Semafor, Trump personally dialed in to an Nvidia board meeting hours before Huang was reinstated to argue for his return. “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board,” White House comms director Steven Cheung told Semafor. “We have to protect our geniuses.” "The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security," Trump said in a post on Truth Social. "The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." The surprise return echoes Sam Altman's return as CEO of OpenAI after the board fired him for a brief five days in 2023 over allegations of dishonesty. Both reinstatements happened around the US Thanksgiving holiday, suggesting that the spirit of forgiveness waxes with the anticipation of that roasted turkey smell wafting through the house. ® Updated at 1607 GMT to include the fact that Trump dialed into a board m

You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify , Apple Music , or YouTube . Those platforms also let you subscribe to The Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live In a week of big stories the biggest one seems to be the fact that everyone from Microsoft to the NSA was dealing with outages , and here's what might be the worst part: It doesn't seem to be AI, nor hostile countries intent on destroying our infrastructure. Unfortunately for all of us, what the past week of outages reveal is that – as we discussed on The Kettle less than a month ago – all of our essential tech infrastructure is basically held together with duct tape and twine. Join host Brandon Vigliarolo , cybersecurity editor Jessica Lyons , and open source reporter Liam Proven to discuss what comes next, and whether we can fix any of this without tearing all of it out and starting from scratch. item.title: COP31 collapse has shattered the pretence of a global climate consensus
item.description: A closing plenary session at the COP31 climate summit on 22 November AP Photo/Khalil Hamra/Alamy A deep rift among nations on how to tackle climate change, and whether the global economy can be weaned off fossil fuels, was exposed after the spectacular collapse of talks at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. After a tortuous fortnight of negotiations, COP31 ended in disarray late on 22 November after countries including the UK and the EU refused to agree to a political accord that failed to mention fossil fuels. Read more Can everyone live a ‘good life’ without destroying the planet? The Antalya pact would have seen countries officially recognise that the world is on course to exceed 1.5°C degrees of warming and promise to limit the scale of the overshoot as far as possible. It also would have committed nations to increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035, a key target for climate campaigners who see electrification as the route away from fossil-fuel dependency. Advertisement But the draft agreement proved unacceptable to many countries, including the UK, the EU and some small island nations, after all mentions of fossil fuels were omitted at the behest of fossil fuel-dependent nations such as Saudi Arabia and Russia. Failing to mention fossil fuels explicitly in the text would have marked a backwards step for the climate process, the EU argued. At COP28 in Dubai three years ago, nations agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels” , but since then, attempts to strengthen the language or clarify how this transition will take place have been blocked by petrostates. Alden Meyer at the climate think tank E3G says the talks were subjected to a “brutish” strategy from fossil fuel-exporting states to “systematically block” any reference to the COP28 deal. “They clearly have buyer’s remorse about that agreement. They never were happy about it.” Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter The EU also took issue with a paragraph inserted at the behest of Saudi Arabia – which leads the 22-member Arab group of countries – calling for the rapid growth of carbon capture and storage technologies to the gigatonne scale by 2035. Carbon capture and storage technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and many sceptics are concerned that focusing on them will justify the continued use of fossil fuels and distract from the deep emissions cuts necessary for controlling climate change. Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, claimed the negotiations had been “hijacked by fossil fuel producers” and said the EU would “not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels”. Parties also vented their frustration at the hosts, Turkey and Australia, with the joint presidency leading to a sluggish and disjointed negotiating process in the final days of the summit. There was also disquiet from lower-income nations over the lack of new climate finance

item.title: F1 in Las Vegas: You've never seen an F1 race like this before
item.description: Las Vegas welcomed Formula 1 to its streets this past weekend. And for the first time since the event’s inception in 2023 , the Grand Prix delivered on a long-promised spectacle. The racing was closer to an IndyCar oval race than anything F1 fans will have seen since slipstreaming was the order of the day at places like Monza and Hockenheim, back when humans were still landing on the Moon and downforce had yet to fundamentally change racing. The Vegas street circuit—the one that looks like an upside-down pig—is an extreme outlier on the calendar. It has plenty of long straights, so this year’s cars still suffer from energy starvation throughout the lap, as the inadequate size of their lithium-ion hybrid batteries means they become depleted very quickly , leaving the cars on just over half power with their V6 engines operating without the benefit of the hybrid’s electric motor. But the 17 turns are mostly all low speed, so there’s no risk of seeing the cars driving demoralizingly slowly through corners that are supposed to test one’s mettle . Read full article Comments

item.title: Trump says he won't allow US companies to build datacenters abroad
item.description: US President Donald Trump has threatened a "tremendous tax" on American companies building datacenters overseas, arguing that the infrastructure should stay at home to preserve the country's AI lead over China. Speaking at a White House press conference after returning from the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Trump portrayed AI leadership as a contest America could not afford to lose. Trump went on to say that "we're not going to allow our companies to build datacenters outside of our country," adding that "they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else and it was very destructive to our country." The threat appeared to catch even his own administration unbriefed. "I haven't even said that to my people, but I'm telling them now," Trump said. The Official White House Rapid Response account posted a video clip on X. We asked the White House if the president intends to follow through, and we will let you know if we get an answer. Trump said: "We're not going to allow companies to build datacenters in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them. We want them to do it here." The threat comes amid concerns that Chinese entities were able to use Nvidia's cutting-edge GPUs for training AI models by accessing cloud services hosted in third countries. The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued new rules to try and crack down on this practice last week. "We're not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, as China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," Trump repeated. "We're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it. They want to build that one in Finland, and we're not allowing that to happen," he added. Google is expanding its facilities in Finland, including one recently in the news because the developer had reportedly illegally felled 250,000 trees to make way for it. Such a policy seems unlikely to be allowed by Congress, where both houses will be under the control of the Democrats when the new term begins in January. Amazon, Google, and Microsoft already operate global datacenter networks to serve customers in different regions. Restrictions on further overseas construction would complicate those businesses. Omdia chief analyst Roy Illsley expressed doubt that this is a serious threat. "There will be ways around that if he does impose some executive order, and the ability to build datacenters is not just an American skill, many countries can build them, it is the equipment in them that is mostly US," he told The Register . item.title: I’m planning my first dark sky trip, and all because this educational star projector showed me what I’m missing
item.description: I didn’t expect much as I unboxed the Brainstorm Night Sky; after all, I’m significantly older than this educational star projector’s target audience. Perhaps I’d come away with a sense of wonder and delight, coupled with mild irritation at having to hunt down three AA batteries to power it. Instead, I was filled with envy as the Brainstorm Night Sky reminded me just what I was missing, thanks to the rigors of light pollution . A few minutes after powering it down, I was already making plans for my first dark sky trip, yearning for a view that rivaled the Brainstorm’s cosmic images. Brainstorm Night Sky Projector review Whatever your age, the Brainstorm Night Sky is so simple to use The Brainstorm Night Sky projector comes with four or six slides, depending on whether you buy the blue or gray version (Image credit: Chris McMullen) Draw the curtains, press the Night Sky’s single button (tilting the projector and twisting the focus as appropriate) and it projects a circular image onto a ceiling or wall. Press the button again and the projection slowly begins to rotate, slowly but stutter-free. It really is that simple to operate and, aimed at budding astronomers aged eight or above, it's reasonably lightweight without feeling flimsy. Depending on the model you buy, you’ll get four or six interchangeable slides. (Image credit: Chris McMullen) Specifications Weight: 14.8 oz (420 g) Bulb type: Non-specified Laser: No Control: On-unit Rotation: Yes, one speed Projection area: Up to 8.2 ft (2.5 m) Sleep timer: Yes (30 mins) Power: 3x AA batteries Speaker: No I was initially a little surprised by the size of the projection: at up to 8.2 feet (2.5 m) wide it’s not going to fill an entire ceiling. It also switches off after 30 minutes, a limit that can’t be disabled, so if you’re looking to put on your own space-themed party this is not the projector for you. But it’s on point for home education and, priced from $49.99, the Brainstorm Night Sky projector won’t break the bank. There’s minimal distortion around the edge of the images; the planets are spherical from the word go, unlike some projectors where I’ve had to tweak them to stop Mars turning into an egg. And I never once had to crane my neck because half the solar system had been projected onto a bookcase. item.title: What did the Soviet Union's final deep space probe actually see on Mars?
item.description:
Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

On July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket. The spacecraft's mission included the study of Mars and the Martian moon Phobos, with a planned close approach and deployment of landing probes, and over the next several months, the spacecraft successfully captured more than three dozen images of Phobos during its time in service. However, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft. Adding to the mystery were objects in some of the final photographs dispatched by the doomed spacecraft, which seemed to show an elongated shadow beneath the probe — a strange twist in one of the Soviet Union's final space missions, and one that soon gave rise to conspiracy theories about what the fate of Phobos 2 might have been. So what caused the odd-looking appearance of the shadow in the final images captured by Phobos 2, and what was the real reason behind the spacecraft's sudden failure? Last of the Soviet space explorers Originally, the Soviet Union had planned for Phobos 2 to reach the Red Planet by late January 1989, after which the spacecraft would begin collecting data about the Martian environment leading up to its initial contact with Mars' largest moon in early June. A model of one of the Phobos spacecraft on display in the Memorial Museum of Cosmonautics in Moscow, Russia. (Image credit: Музей Космонавтики from Россия, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons) To say that a lot hinged on the success of the mission would be an understatement, given the unfortunate fate of the probe's predecessor, Phobos 1, which went offline on Sept. 2, 1988, after a faulty command sequence was initiated while the spacecraft was on its way to Mars. The stakes were almost immediately raised as Phobos 2 arrived in orbit around Mars on Jan. 30, 1989 , when one of the probe's three onboard flight system processors was found to have gone offline, with another already experiencing technical issues. Over the course of the next several weeks, Phobos 2 was able to overcome some of these setbacks and successfully began sending useful scientific data about the Martian environment back to Earth. By March, all the probe's science instruments appeared to be functioning normally, and despite the earlier loss of one of its processors, the remaining two had continued to facilitate control of the spacecraft by its Soviet ground control team. An image of Phobos captured by the Soviet Union's Phobos 2 probe. (Image credit: Roscosmos) Unexplained failure That all changed on March 27, 1989, as Phobos 2 prepared to capture navigational ima
